Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Smallest angle of a triangle with sides $5,6,10$
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = 5\text{ cm}$, $BC = 6\text{ cm}$ and $AC = 10\text{ cm}$. Calculate the size of the smallest angle.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Identify the smallest side and use the cosine rule on the angle opposite that side: for a triangle with sides $a,b,c$ and opposite angles $A,B,C$, $a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2bc\cos A$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&\text{The smallest side is }AB=5\text{ cm, so the smallest angle is }\angle C\text{ opposite }AB.\\&\text{By the cosine rule in }\triangle ABC:\\&AB^{2}=BC^{2}+AC^{2}-2(BC)(AC)\cos C.\\&5^{2}=6^{2}+10^{2}-2\cdot6\cdot10\cos C\\&25=36+100-120\cos C\\&120\cos C=136-25=111\\&\cos C=\dfrac{111}{120}\approx0.925.\\&C\approx\cos^{-1}(0.925)\approx22^\circ\ (\text{to the nearest degree}).\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Largest angle of a triangle with sides $9.3,6.2,12.7$
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = 9.3\text{ cm}$, $BC = 6.2\text{ cm}$ and $AC = 12.7\text{ cm}$. Calculate the size of the largest angle.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Identify the largest side and use the cosine rule on the angle opposite that side: $a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2bc\cos A$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&\text{Largest side is }AC=12.7\text{ cm, so the largest angle is }\angle B.\\&\text{By the cosine rule:}\\&AC^{2}=AB^{2}+BC^{2}-2(AB)(BC)\cos B.\\&12.7^{2}=9.3^{2}+6.2^{2}-2\cdot9.3\cdot6.2\cos B.\\&161.29=86.49+38.44-115.32\cos B\\&161.29=124.93-115.32\cos B\\&-115.32\cos B=161.29-124.93=36.36\\&\cos B=-\dfrac{36.36}{115.32}\approx-0.315.\\&B\approx\cos^{-1}(-0.315)\approx108^\circ\ (\text{to the nearest degree}).\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Largest angle when sides are in ratio $2:3:4$
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: The lengths of the sides of a triangle are in the ratio $2:3:4$. Calculate the size of the largest angle.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Let the sides be $2k,3k,4k$. The largest angle is opposite $4k$. Apply the cosine rule: $(4k)^{2}=(2k)^{2}+(3k)^{2}-2(2k)(3k)\cos\theta$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&\text{Let the sides be }2k,3k,4k,\ \text{largest angle }=\theta\text{ opposite }4k.\\&\text{Cosine rule: }(4k)^{2}=(2k)^{2}+(3k)^{2}-2(2k)(3k)\cos\theta.\\&16k^{2}=4k^{2}+9k^{2}-12k^{2}\cos\theta\\&16k^{2}=13k^{2}-12k^{2}\cos\theta\\&12k^{2}\cos\theta=13k^{2}-16k^{2}=-3k^{2}\\&\cos\theta=-\dfrac{3}{12}=-\dfrac14.\\&\theta\approx\cos^{-1}\!\left(-\dfrac14\right)\approx104^\circ\ (\text{to the nearest degree}).\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Finding $x$ using cosine rule with $\angle BAC=60^\circ$
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = (x - 3)\text{ cm}$, $BC = (x + 3)\text{ cm}$, $AC = 8\text{ cm}$ and $\angle BAC = 60^\circ$. Use the cosine rule to find the value of $x$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the cosine rule with side $BC$ opposite angle $A$: $BC^{2}=AB^{2}+AC^{2}-2(AB)(AC)\cos60^\circ$. Substitute the given expressions and solve the resulting quadratic equation for $x$.

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Ambiguous case to find $\angle ABC$ and then $AC$
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: Triangle $$ABC$$ is such that $$AB = 4\text{ cm}$$, $$BC = 6\text{ cm}$$ and $$\angle ACB = 36^\circ$$. Show that one of the possible values of $$\angle ABC$$ is $$25.8^\circ$$ (to 3 s.f.). Using this value, calculate the length of $$AC$$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the sine rule with $$AB$$ opposite $$\angle C$$ and $$BC$$ opposite $$\angle A$$ to find two possible values of $$\angle A$$. For each, compute $$\angle B=180^\circ-A-36^\circ$$ and show one is approximately $$25.8^\circ$$. Then, using $$B\approx25.8^\circ$$ and its corresponding $$A$$, apply the sine rule again to find $$AC$$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\text{Sine rule: }\dfrac{AB}{\sin C}=\dfrac{BC}{\sin A}\Rightarrow\dfrac{4}{\sin36^\circ}=\dfrac{6}{\sin A}\Rightarrow\sin A=\dfrac{6\sin36^\circ}{4}=\dfrac32\sin36^\circ\approx\dfrac32\times0.588\approx0.882\Rightarrow A\approx61.9^\circ\text{ or }A'\approx180^\circ-61.9^\circ=118.1^\circ.$$ $$\text{Then }B=180^\circ-36^\circ-61.9^\circ\approx82.1^\circ,\ B'=180^\circ-36^\circ-118.1^\circ\approx25.9^\circ\approx25.8^\circ\text{ (to 3 s.f.), as required. For }B'\approx25.8^\circ\text{ we have }A'\approx118.2^\circ.$$ $$\text{Using this pair in the sine rule, }\dfrac{BC}{\sin A'}=\dfrac{AC}{\sin B'}\Rightarrow\dfrac{6}{\sin118.2^\circ}=\dfrac{AC}{\sin25.8^\circ}\Rightarrow AC=6\dfrac{\sin25.8^\circ}{\sin118.2^\circ}\approx6\dfrac{0.435}{0.881}\approx2.96\text{ cm (to 3 s.f.).}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Largest angles in two possible triangles
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: Two triangles $$ABC$$ are such that $$AB = 4.5\text{ cm}$$, $$BC = 6.8\text{ cm}$$ and $$\angle ACB = 30^\circ$$. Work out the value of the largest angle in each of the triangles.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the sine rule with $$AB$$ opposite $$\angle C$$ and $$BC$$ opposite $$\angle A$$ to find two possible angles $$A_1$$ and $$A_2=180^\circ-A_1$$. For each triangle compute $$B=180^\circ-A-C$$, then identify, for each case, which of $$A,B,C$$ is largest.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\dfrac{AB}{\sin C}=\dfrac{BC}{\sin A}\Rightarrow\dfrac{4.5}{\sin30^\circ}=\dfrac{6.8}{\sin A}\Rightarrow\dfrac{4.5}{\tfrac12}=\dfrac{6.8}{\sin A}\Rightarrow9=\dfrac{6.8}{\sin A}\Rightarrow\sin A=\dfrac{6.8}{9}\approx0.756.$$ $$\Rightarrow A_1\approx\sin^{-1}(0.756)\approx49.0^\circ,\ A_2\approx180^\circ-49.0^\circ=131.0^\circ.$$ $$\text{For }A_1\approx49.0^\circ,\ B_1=180^\circ-30^\circ-49.0^\circ\approx101.0^\circ,\ \text{so the largest angle is }B_1\approx101^\circ.$$ $$\text{For }A_2\approx131.0^\circ,\ B_2=180^\circ-30^\circ-131.0^\circ\approx19.0^\circ,\ \text{so the largest angle is }A_2\approx131^\circ.$$ $$\text{Thus the largest angles are approximately }101^\circ\text{ and }131^\circ\text{ in the two triangles.}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In a crane arm model, a crane arm $AB$ of length $80\text{ m}$ is anchored at point $B$ at an angle of $40^\circ$ to the horizontal. A wrecking ball is suspended on a cable of length $60\text{ m}$ from $A$. Find the angle $x$ through which the wrecking ball rotates as it passes the two points level with the base of the crane arm at $B$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Drop a perpendicular from $A$ to the horizontal line through $B$ at $H$. Use right-triangle trigonometry to find the vertical height $AH$, then apply $\cos\theta=\dfrac{AH}{AD}$ in triangle $ADH$ where $AD=60\text{ m}$ is the cable and $\theta$ is the angle from the vertical. The total rotation $x$ is $2\theta$ since the motion is symmetric about the vertical.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\text{Let }H\text{ be the foot of the perpendicular from }A\text{ to the horizontal through }B.\ \text{Then }AH=AB\sin40^\circ=80\sin40^\circ.\ \text{When the ball is level with }B,\ \triangle ADH\text{ is right-angled with }AD=60\text{ m and }AH\text{ opposite the horizontal. Let }\angle DAH=\theta.\ \text{Then }\cos\theta=\dfrac{AH}{AD}=\dfrac{80\sin40^\circ}{60}\Rightarrow\theta=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{80\sin40^\circ}{60}\right)\approx31.0^\circ.\ \text{The wrecking ball passes through two symmetric positions on either side of the vertical, so }x=2\theta\approx2\times31.0^\circ\approx62.0^\circ\text{ (to 3 s.f.).}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Modelling assumption for wrecking ball motion
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In a crane arm model, a crane arm $AB$ of length $80\text{ m}$ is anchored at point $B$ at an angle of $40^\circ$ to the horizontal. A wrecking ball is suspended on a cable of length $60\text{ m}$ from $A$. Write down one modelling assumption you have made.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Think about physical simplifications that make the geometry work: the cable is of fixed length and always taut, the ball is treated as a point mass, air resistance is ignored, and the motion is confined to a single vertical plane.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: State that the cable is light, inextensible and remains taut so that the wrecking ball moves in a circular arc of constant radius $60\text{ m}$ about $A$.

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: $$\text{In }\triangle ABC,\ AB=x\text{ cm},\ BC=(4-x)\text{ cm},\ \angle BAC=y,\ \angle BCA=30^\circ.\ \text{Given }\sin y=\frac{1}{\sqrt2},\ \text{show that }x=4(\sqrt2-1).$$
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: $$\text{Use the Sine Rule: }\dfrac{AB}{\sin C}=\dfrac{BC}{\sin A}\ \text{and substitute }\sin30^\circ=\frac12,\ \sin y=\frac1{\sqrt2}.$$
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\text{In }\triangle ABC,\ &\angle C=30^\circ,\ \angle A=y\\[4pt]\text{By the Sine Rule: }\frac{AB}{\sin C}&=\frac{BC}{\sin A}\\[4pt]\frac{x}{\sin30^\circ}&=\frac{4-x}{\sin y}\\[4pt]\frac{x}{\tfrac12}&=\frac{4-x}{\tfrac1{\sqrt2}}\\[4pt]2x&=\sqrt2(4-x)\\2x&=4\sqrt2-\sqrt2\,x\\x(2+\sqrt2)&=4\sqrt2\\[4pt]x&=\frac{4\sqrt2}{2+\sqrt2}\\[4pt]\text{Rationalise: }x&=\frac{4\sqrt2(2-\sqrt2)}{(2+\sqrt2)(2-\sqrt2)}=\frac{4\sqrt2(2-\sqrt2)}{4-2}\\[4pt]x&=\frac{8\sqrt2-8}{2}=4\sqrt2-4\\[4pt]\therefore\ x&=4(\sqrt2-1)\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Find the height of the building
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: $$\text{A surveyor measures the angles of elevation of the top of a building from two points on level ground 15 m apart. The angles are }40^\circ\text{ and }52^\circ.\ \text{Find the height of the building.}$$
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: $$\text{Let the distance from the nearer point (52°) to the building be }d.\ \text{Then the other distance is }d+15.\ \text{Use }\tan=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}.$$
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\text{Let the height be }h\text{ m. Let the nearer point (angle }52^\circ\text{) be }d\text{ m from the base.}\\[4pt]\tan52^\circ&=\frac{h}{d}\ \Rightarrow\ h=d\tan52^\circ\\[4pt]\tan40^\circ&=\frac{h}{d+15}\ \Rightarrow\ h=(d+15)\tan40^\circ\\[6pt]\text{Equate the two expressions for }h:\\d\tan52^\circ&=(d+15)\tan40^\circ\\d(\tan52^\circ-\tan40^\circ)&=15\tan40^\circ\\d&=\frac{15\tan40^\circ}{\tan52^\circ-\tan40^\circ}\\[6pt]\text{Then }h&=d\tan52^\circ=\frac{15\tan40^\circ\tan52^\circ}{\tan52^\circ-\tan40^\circ}\\[6pt]\tan40^\circ\approx0.8391,\ \tan52^\circ\approx1.2799\ \Rightarrow\ h&\approx36.5437\\[4pt]\therefore\ \text{Height }h&\approx36.5\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: $$\text{In }\triangle ABC,\ AB=x\text{ cm},\ AC=(5+x)\text{ cm},\ \angle BAC=150^\circ.\ \text{Area}=3\tfrac34\text{ cm}^2.$$
In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = (2 - x)\text{ cm}$, $BC = (x + 1)\text{ cm}$ and $\angle ABC = 120^\circ$. a Show that $AC^2 = x^2 - x + 7$. b Find the value of $x$ for which $AC$ has a minimum value.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Apply the cosine rule with the included angle $120^\circ$ to get an expression for $AC^2$ in terms of $x$, then complete the square for $x^2 - x + 7$ to locate the minimum.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned} &\textbf{(a)}\ \text{By the cosine rule with angle at }B: \\ &AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 - 2(AB)(BC)\cos120^\circ. \\ &AB^2 = (2-x)^2 = x^2 - 4x + 4,\quad BC^2 = (x+1)^2 = x^2 + 2x + 1. \\ &AB\cdot BC = (2-x)(x+1). \\ &\cos120^\circ = -\frac12 \Rightarrow -2(AB)(BC)\cos120^\circ = -2(2-x)(x+1)\left(-\frac12\right) = (2-x)(x+1). \\ &\Rightarrow AC^2 = (x^2 - 4x + 4) + (x^2 + 2x + 1) + (2-x)(x+1). \\ &(2-x)(x+1) = 2x + 2 - x^2 - x = -x^2 + x + 2. \\ &\Rightarrow AC^2 = (x^2 - 4x + 4) + (x^2 + 2x + 1) + (-x^2 + x + 2) \\ &\qquad= x^2 - x + 7,\ \text{as required}. \\ &\textbf{(b)}\ AC^2 = x^2 - x + 7. \text{ Complete the square:} \\ &x^2 - x + 7 = \left(x - \frac12\right)^2 - \left(\frac12\right)^2 + 7 = \left(x - \frac12\right)^2 + \frac{27}{4}. \\ &\left(x - \frac12\right)^2 \ge 0\ \text{for all }x,\ \text{so }AC^2\text{ is minimal when }x - \frac12 = 0. \\ &\Rightarrow x = \frac12. \end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In triangle $ABC$ such that $BC = 5\sqrt2\text{ cm}$, $\angle ABC = 30^\circ$ and $\angle BAC = \theta$, where $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt5}{8}$. Work out the length of $AC$, giving your answer in the form $a\sqrt b$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the sine rule with side $BC$ opposite $\angle BAC=\theta$ and side $AC$ opposite $\angle ABC=30^\circ$, substituting $\sin\theta=\tfrac{\sqrt5}{8}$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned} &\text{By the sine rule: }\frac{BC}{\sin\angle BAC} = \frac{AC}{\sin\angle ABC}. \\ &\Rightarrow \frac{5\sqrt2}{\sin\theta} = \frac{AC}{\sin30^\circ}. \\ &\sin\theta = \frac{\sqrt5}{8},\ \sin30^\circ = \frac12. \\ &\Rightarrow \frac{5\sqrt2}{\sqrt5/8} = \frac{AC}{1/2}. \\ &\frac{5\sqrt2}{\sqrt5/8} = 5\sqrt2 \cdot \frac{8}{\sqrt5} = \frac{40\sqrt2}{\sqrt5}. \\ &\Rightarrow \frac{40\sqrt2}{\sqrt5} = 2AC \Rightarrow AC = \frac{20\sqrt2}{\sqrt5}. \\ &\text{Rationalise: }\frac{20\sqrt2}{\sqrt5} = 20\sqrt{\frac{2}{5}} = \frac{20\sqrt{10}}{5} = 4\sqrt{10}\text{ cm}. \end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: The perimeter of $\triangle ABC$ is $15\text{ cm}$. Given that $AB = 7\text{ cm}$ and $\angle BAC = 60^\circ$, find the lengths of $AC$ and $BC$ and the area of the triangle.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Let $AC = x$ and use the perimeter to write $BC$ in terms of $x$. Then apply the cosine rule with $\angle BAC = 60^\circ$ opposite $BC$ to solve for $x$, and finally use $A=\tfrac12 ab\sin C$ with sides $AB$ and $AC$ around $\angle BAC$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned} &\text{Let }AC = x\text{ cm}. \text{ Perimeter }AB+BC+AC=15\Rightarrow 7+(8-x)+x=15\Rightarrow BC=8-x\text{ cm}. \\ &\text{Use the cosine rule with angle at }A: \\ &BC^2 = AB^2 + AC^2 - 2(AB)(AC)\cos60^\circ. \\ &(8-x)^2 = 7^2 + x^2 - 2\cdot7\cdot x\cdot\frac12 = 49 + x^2 - 7x. \\ &64 - 16x + x^2 = 49 + x^2 - 7x. \\ &64 - 16x = 49 - 7x \Rightarrow 15 = 9x \Rightarrow x = \frac{15}{9} = \frac53\text{ cm}. \\ &\Rightarrow AC = \frac53\text{ cm},\quad BC = 8 - \frac53 = \frac{24-5}{3} = \frac{19}{3}\text{ cm}. \\ &\text{Area of } \triangle ABC: A = \tfrac12\cdot AB\cdot AC\cdot\sin\angle BAC. \\ &A = \tfrac12\cdot7\cdot\frac53\cdot\sin60^\circ = \frac{35}{6}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} = \frac{35\sqrt3}{12}\text{ cm}^2 \approx 5.05\text{ cm}^2. \end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In the triangle $ABC$, $AB = 14\text{ cm}$, $BC = 12\text{ cm}$ and $CA = 15\text{ cm}$. a Find the size of angle $C$, giving your answer to $3$ s.f. b Find the area of triangle $ABC$, giving your answer in cm$^2$ to $3$ s.f.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the cosine rule with side $AB$ opposite angle $C$ to find $\cos C$ and hence $C$. Then use $A=\tfrac12 ab\sin C$ with sides $BC$ and $CA$ around angle $C$ to find the area.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned} &\textbf{(a)}\ \text{For angle }C=\angle ACB\text{, the opposite side is }AB=14\text{ cm, with adjacent sides }BC=12\text{ cm and }CA=15\text{ cm}. \\ &\text{Cosine rule: }AB^2 = BC^2 + CA^2 - 2(BC)(CA)\cos C. \\ &14^2 = 12^2 + 15^2 - 2\cdot12\cdot15\cos C. \\ &196 = 144 + 225 - 360\cos C = 369 - 360\cos C. \\ &360\cos C = 369 - 196 = 173 \Rightarrow \cos C = \frac{173}{360} \approx 0.4806. \\ &\Rightarrow C \approx \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{173}{360}\right) \approx 61.3^\circ\ \text{(to 3 s.f.)}. \\ &\textbf{(b)}\ \text{Area }A = \tfrac12\cdot BC\cdot CA\cdot\sin C = \tfrac12\cdot12\cdot15\cdot\sin C = 90\sin C. \\ &\sin C = \sqrt{1-\cos^2 C} = \sqrt{1-\left(\frac{173}{360}\right)^2} \approx 0.876. \\ &\Rightarrow A \approx 90\times0.876 \approx 78.8\text{ cm}^2\ \text{(to 3 s.f.)}. \end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: A flower bed is in the shape of a quadrilateral as shown in the diagram. a Find the sizes of angles $DAB$ and $BCD$. b Find the total area of the flower bed. c Find the length of the diagonal $AC$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the cosine rule in $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle BCD$ to get the two angles asked in part (a). Use $\tfrac12ab\sin C$ in each triangle to add their areas for part (b). For part (c), first find the angles at $B$ in $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle BCD$, add them to get $\angle ABC$, then use the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$ to find $AC$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\textbf{(a)}\ \text{In }\triangle ABD: BD^2=AB^2+AD^2-2(AB)(AD)\cos\angle DAB\Rightarrow5.9^2=4.2^2+2.1^2-2(4.2)(2.1)\cos\angle DAB\Rightarrow\cos\angle DAB=\dfrac{4.2^2+2.1^2-5.9^2}{2\cdot4.2\cdot2.1}\approx-0.723\Rightarrow\angle DAB\approx136^\circ.\ \text{In }\triangle BCD: BD^2=BC^2+CD^2-2(BC)(CD)\cos\angle BCD\Rightarrow5.9^2=7.5^2+3.5^2-2(7.5)(3.5)\cos\angle BCD\Rightarrow\cos\angle BCD=\dfrac{7.5^2+3.5^2-5.9^2}{2\cdot7.5\cdot3.5}\approx0.642\Rightarrow\angle BCD\approx50.1^\circ.$$\ $$\textbf{(b)}\ \text{Area of }\triangle ABD=\tfrac12\cdot AB\cdot AD\sin\angle DAB=\tfrac12\cdot4.2\cdot2.1\sin136^\circ\approx3.04\text{ m}^2.\ \text{Area of }\triangle BCD=\tfrac12\cdot BC\cdot CD\sin\angle BCD=\tfrac12\cdot7.5\cdot3.5\sin50.1^\circ\approx10.1\text{ m}^2.\ \text{Total area}\approx3.04+10.1\approx13.1\text{ m}^2.$$\ $$\textbf{(c)}\ \text{In }\triangle ABD:\ \cos\angle ABD=\dfrac{AB^2+BD^2-AD^2}{2(AB)(BD)}=\dfrac{4.2^2+5.9^2-2.1^2}{2\cdot4.2\cdot5.9}\approx0.969\Rightarrow\angle ABD\approx14.2^\circ.\ \text{In }\triangle BCD:\ \cos\angle CBD=\dfrac{BC^2+BD^2-CD^2}{2(BC)(BD)}=\dfrac{7.5^2+5.9^2-3.5^2}{2\cdot7.5\cdot5.9}\approx0.891\Rightarrow\angle CBD\approx27.1^\circ.\ \Rightarrow\angle ABC=\angle ABD+\angle CBD\approx14.2^\circ+27.1^\circ\approx41.3^\circ.\ \text{Now in }\triangle ABC:\ AC^2=AB^2+BC^2-2(AB)(BC)\cos\angle ABC=4.2^2+7.5^2-2(4.2)(7.5)\cos41.3^\circ\Rightarrow AC\approx5.15\text{ m}.$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.subtopic_name: Graphs of sine, cosine and tangent
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: $$\text{Sketch the graph of }y=\cos\theta\text{ in the interval }-180^\circ\le\theta\le180^\circ.$$
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: $$\text{Recall cosine is an even function with period }360^\circ\text{ and amplitude }1.$$
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\text{Key properties:}\\\text{Amplitude}&=1\\\text{Period}&=360^\circ\\\text{Even function }&\Rightarrow\text{ symmetric about the }y\text{-axis}\\[6pt]\text{Key points:}\\\theta=-180^\circ&:\ y=\cos(-180^\circ)=-1\\\theta=-90^\circ&:\ y=0\\\theta=0^\circ&:\ y=1\\\theta=90^\circ&:\ y=0\\\theta=180^\circ&:\ y=-1\\[6pt]\text{Plot these points accurately and join them with a smooth cosine curve.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: $$\text{Sketch the graph of }y=\tan\theta\text{ in the interval }-180^\circ\le\theta\le180^\circ.$$
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: $$\text{Recall tangent has period }180^\circ\text{ and vertical asymptotes where }\cos\theta=0.$$
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\text{Key properties:}\\\text{Period}&=180^\circ\\\text{Odd function }&\Rightarrow\text{ symmetric about the origin}\\[6pt]\text{Vertical asymptotes:}\\\theta&=-90^\circ,\ 90^\circ\\[6pt]\text{Key points:}\\\theta=-135^\circ&:\ y=\tan(-135^\circ)=1\\\theta=-45^\circ&:\ y=-1\\\theta=0^\circ&:\ y=0\\\theta=45^\circ&:\ y=1\\\theta=135^\circ&:\ y=-1\\[6pt]\text{Draw increasing branches between the asymptotes, passing through the origin.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.subtopic_name: Graphs of sine, cosine and tangent
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: $$\text{The graph shows the curve }y=\cos(x+30^\circ),\ -360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ.\ \text{(a) Write down the coordinates where the curve crosses the x-axis. (b) Find the coordinates where the curve crosses the y-axis.}$$
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\textbf{(a) x-axis crossings:}\\\cos(x+30^\circ)&=0\\x+30^\circ&=90^\circ+180^\circ k\\x&=60^\circ+180^\circ k\\-360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ\Rightarrow x&=-300^\circ,\ -120^\circ,\ 60^\circ,\ 240^\circ\\\text{Coordinates: }&(-300^\circ,0),(-120^\circ,0),(60^\circ,0),(240^\circ,0)\\[6pt]\textbf{(b) y-axis crossing:}\\x&=0\\y&=\cos(30^\circ)=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\\\text{Coordinate: }&(0,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2})\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.subtopic_name: Graphs of sine, cosine and tangent
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: $$\text{The graph shows }y=\sin(x+k),\ -360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ,\ \text{where }k\text{ is a constant. (a) Find one possible value of }k.\ \text{(b) State whether there is more than one possible value of }k\text{ and give a reason.}$$
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: $$\text{Use a key feature such as a maximum or x-axis crossing and compare with }y=\sin x.$}$
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\textbf{(a) One possible value of }k:\\\text{From the graph, a maximum occurs at }x&=60^\circ\\\text{For }y=\sin(x+k),\text{ maxima occur when }x+k&=90^\circ\\k&=90^\circ-60^\circ=30^\circ\\[6pt]\textbf{(b) More than one value?}\\\sin(x+k)\text{ has period }360^\circ&\Rightarrow k=30^\circ+360^\circ n,\ n\in\mathbb{Z}\\\text{So there are infinitely many possible values of }k.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: Triangle $ABC$ has area $10\text{ cm}^2$. $AB = 6\text{ cm}$, $BC = 8\text{ cm}$ and $\angle ABC$ is obtuse. Find: a the size of $\angle ABC$ b the length of $AC$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use $A=\tfrac12 ab\sin C$ to find $\sin B$ and choose the obtuse angle; then use the cosine rule to find $AC$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $10=\tfrac12\cdot6\cdot8\sin B\Rightarrow10=24\sin B\Rightarrow\sin B=\tfrac{5}{12}\Rightarrow B=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\tfrac{5}{12}\right)\approx24^\circ,\ \text{but }B\text{ is obtuse so }B=180^\circ-24^\circ=156^\circ.\ \text{Next }AC^2=6^2+8^2-2\cdot6\cdot8\cos156^\circ=36+64-96\cos156^\circ,\ \cos156^\circ=-\cos24^\circ\approx-0.9135\Rightarrow AC^2\approx187.7\Rightarrow AC\approx13.7\text{ cm}.$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In triangle $a$, the three sides are $2.4\text{ cm}$, $3\text{ cm}$ and $1.2\text{ cm}$, and angle $x$ is opposite the $2.4\text{ cm}$ side. Find the size of $x$ and the area of the triangle.

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In triangle $b$, two sides are $6\text{ cm}$ and $5\text{ cm}$ and the included angles at the other two vertices are $x^\circ$ and $80^\circ$ as shown. Find the size of $x$ and the area of the triangle.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the sine rule with side $6\text{ cm}$ opposite $80^\circ$ to find the top angle, then use the angle sum of a triangle to get $x$, and finally $A=\tfrac12 ab\sin C$ with sides $6$ and $5$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: \text{Let the top angle be }B.\ \dfrac{6}{\sin80^\circ}=\dfrac{5}{\sin B}\Rightarrow\sin B=\dfrac{5\sin80^\circ}{6}\approx0.821\Rightarrow B\approx55.2^\circ.\ \text{Angles in a triangle: }x=180^\circ-80^\circ-B\approx180^\circ-80^\circ-55.2^\circ\approx44.8^\circ.\ \text{Area}=\tfrac12\cdot6\cdot5\sin B\approx\tfrac12\cdot6\cdot5\cdot\sin55.2^\circ\approx12.3\text{ cm}^2.$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In triangle $c$, two sides are $3\text{ cm}$ and $5\text{ cm}$ and the angle at the end of the $3\text{ cm}$ side is $40^\circ$, with $x^\circ$ the angle between the $3\text{ cm}$ and $5\text{ cm}$ sides. Find the size of $x$ and the area of the triangle.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the sine rule with sides $5\text{ cm}$ and $3\text{ cm}$ opposite the other two angles to find the third angle, then use angle sum to get $x$, and finish with $A=\tfrac12 ab\sin C$ using the sides $3$ and $5$ and included angle $x$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: \text{Let the angles opposite }5\text{ cm},3\text{ cm},\text{ and the base be }40^\circ,C,\text{ and }x\text{ respectively. By the sine rule }\dfrac{5}{\sin40^\circ}=\dfrac{3}{\sin C}\Rightarrow\sin C=\dfrac{3\sin40^\circ}{5}\approx0.386\Rightarrow C\approx22.7^\circ.\ \text{Angles in a triangle: }x=180^\circ-40^\circ-C\approx180^\circ-40^\circ-22.7^\circ\approx117.3^\circ.\ \text{Area}=\tfrac12\cdot3\cdot5\sin x\approx\tfrac12\cdot3\cdot5\cdot\sin117.3^\circ\approx6.66\text{ cm}^2.$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Largest angle and area from three sides
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: The sides of a triangle are $3\text{ cm}$, $5\text{ cm}$ and $7\text{ cm}$ respectively. Show that the largest angle is $120^\circ$, and find the area of the triangle.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the cosine rule with side $7\text{ cm}$ opposite the largest angle, then use $A=\tfrac12 ab\sin C$ with sides $3$ and $5$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$7^2 = 3^2 + 5^2 - 2\cdot3\cdot5\cos C \Rightarrow 49 = 9 + 25 - 30\cos C \Rightarrow 49 = 34 - 30\cos C \Rightarrow 15 = -30\cos C \Rightarrow \cos C = -\tfrac12 \Rightarrow C = 120^\circ.$$ $$\text{Area} = \tfrac12\cdot3\cdot5\sin120^\circ = \tfrac{15}{2}\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = \tfrac{15\sqrt3}{4}\text{ cm}^2.$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = 10\text{ cm}$, $BC = a\sqrt3\text{ cm}$, $AC = 5\sqrt{13}\text{ cm}$ and $\angle ABC = 150^\circ$. Calculate: a the value of $a$ b the exact area of $\triangle ABC$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the cosine rule with side $AC$ opposite $\angle ABC$ to find $a$, then use $A=\tfrac12 ab\sin C$ with sides $AB$ and $BC$ and angle $150^\circ$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\text{Cosine rule: }(5\sqrt{13})^2 = 10^2 + (a\sqrt3)^2 - 2\cdot10\cdot a\sqrt3\cos150^\circ.$$ $$325 = 100 + 3a^2 - 20a\sqrt3\cdot\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) = 100 + 3a^2 + 30a.$$ $$\Rightarrow 3a^2 + 30a + 100 - 325 = 0 \Rightarrow 3a^2 + 30a - 225 = 0 \Rightarrow a^2 + 10a - 75 = 0.$$ $$a = \frac{-10 \pm \sqrt{10^2 - 4\cdot1\cdot(-75)}}{2} = \frac{-10 \pm 20}{2} \Rightarrow a = 5\ (\text{reject }a=-15).$$ $$BC = 5\sqrt3\text{ cm},\ \text{area} = \tfrac12\cdot10\cdot5\sqrt3\sin150^\circ = \tfrac12\cdot10\cdot5\sqrt3\cdot\tfrac12 = 25\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2.$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In a triangle, the largest side has length $2\text{ cm}$ and one of the other sides has length $\sqrt2\text{ cm}$. Given that the area of the triangle is $1\text{ cm}^2$, show that the triangle is right-angled and isosceles.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Let the angle between the sides $2$ and $\sqrt2$ be $\theta$. Use the area formula to find $\theta$, then use the cosine rule to find the third side and the angle opposite the largest side.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$1 = \tfrac12\cdot2\cdot\sqrt2\sin\theta \Rightarrow 1 = \sqrt2\sin\theta \Rightarrow \sin\theta = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}.$$ $$\theta = 45^\circ\ \text{or}\ 135^\circ,\ \text{but if }\theta=135^\circ\text{ the third side would exceed }2\text{ cm, contradicting that }2\text{ is the largest side, so }\theta = 45^\circ.$$ $$\text{Cosine rule for the third side }x:\ x^2 = 2^2 + (\sqrt2)^2 - 2\cdot2\cdot\sqrt2\cos45^\circ = 4 + 2 - 4\sqrt2\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2} = 6 - 4 = 2,$$ $$\Rightarrow x = \sqrt2\text{ cm, so the two smaller sides are both }\sqrt2\text{ cm (isosceles).}$$ $$\text{Angle opposite side }2\text{ (call it }C\text{): } \cos C = \dfrac{\sqrt2^2 + \sqrt2^2 - 2^2}{2\cdot\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2} = \dfrac{2 + 2 - 4}{4} = 0 \Rightarrow C = 90^\circ.$$ $$\text{Thus the triangle is right-angled and isosceles.}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Cosine of angle and area from coordinates
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: The three points $A$, $B$ and $C$, with coordinates $A(0,1)$, $B(3,4)$ and $C(1,3)$ respectively, are joined to form a triangle. a Show that $\cos\angle ACB = -\dfrac45$. b Calculate the area of $\triangle ABC$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Form vectors $\overrightarrow{CA}$ and $\overrightarrow{CB}$ and use the dot product to find $\cos\angle ACB$, then use the coordinate (determinant) formula for the area of a triangle.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\overrightarrow{CA} = A - C = (-1,-2),\ \overrightarrow{CB} = B - C = (2,1).$$ $$\overrightarrow{CA}\cdot\overrightarrow{CB} = (-1)(2) + (-2)(1) = -4,\ |\overrightarrow{CA}| = |\overrightarrow{CB}| = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt5.$$ $$\cos\angle ACB = \dfrac{\overrightarrow{CA}\cdot\overrightarrow{CB}}{|\overrightarrow{CA}||\overrightarrow{CB}|} = \dfrac{-4}{\sqrt5\cdot\sqrt5} = -\dfrac45.$$ $$\text{Area} = \tfrac12\left|x_A(y_B - y_C) + x_B(y_C - y_A) + x_C(y_A - y_B)\right| = \tfrac12\left|0(4-3) + 3(3-1) + 1(1-4)\right|$$ $$= \tfrac12|0 + 6 - 3| = \tfrac12\cdot3 = \tfrac32\text{ square units.}$$

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: A park is in the shape of a triangle $ABC$ as shown. A park keeper walks due north from his hut at $A$ until he reaches point $B$. He then walks on a bearing of $110^\circ$ to point $C$. a Find how far he is from his hut when at point $C$. Give your answer in km to $3$ s.f. b Work out the bearing of the hut from point $C$. Give your answer to the nearest degree. c Work out the area of the park.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use bearings to find $\angle ABC=180^\circ-110^\circ$, then apply the cosine rule to get $AC$; use components or triangle angles to get the bearing of $A$ from $C$; use $A=\tfrac12ab\sin C$ for the area.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: In $\triangle ABC$ we have $AB=1.2$, $BC=1.4$ (in km) and $\angle ABC=180^\circ-110^\circ=70^\circ$ since $BA$ has bearing $180^\circ$ and $BC$ has bearing $110^\circ$; by the cosine rule $AC^2=1.2^2+1.4^2-2(1.2)(1.4)\cos70^\circ\approx2.251\Rightarrow AC\approx1.50\text{ km}$, so he is $1.50\text{ km}$ from his hut; to find the bearing of $A$ from $C$, resolve $BC$: from $B$ to $C$ the east component is $1.4\sin110^\circ\approx1.32$ and the north component is $1.4\cos110^\circ\approx-0.48$, so relative to $A$ we have $C$ at $(E,N)\approx(1.32,1.2-0.48)=(1.32,0.72)$; the vector from $C$ to $A$ has components $(-1.32,-0.72)$, so the bearing of $A$ from $C$ is $\theta\approx241^\circ$ (using $\theta=\operatorname{bearing}=\arg(E,N)$); the area of the park is $A=\tfrac12\cdot1.2\cdot1.4\sin70^\circ\approx0.789\text{ km}^2$.

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: A windmill has four identical triangular sails made from wood. If each triangle has sides of length $12\text{ m}$, $15\text{ m}$ and $20\text{ m}$, work out the total area of wood needed.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: First find the area of one triangle using Heron’s formula with semiperimeter $s$, then multiply by $4$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: For one triangle $a=12$, $b=15$, $c=20$; the semiperimeter is $s=\tfrac{12+15+20}{2}=23.5$; by Heron’s formula the area is $\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}=\sqrt{23.5\times11.5\times8.5\times3.5}\approx89.7\text{ m}^2$; there are $4$ identical sails, so the total area of wood is $4\times89.7\approx359\text{ m}^2$ (to $3$ s.f.).

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: Two points, $A$ and $B$ are on level ground. A church tower at point $C$ has an angle of elevation from $A$ of $15^\circ$ and an angle of elevation from $B$ of $32^\circ$. $A$ and $B$ are both on the same side of $C$, and $A$, $B$ and $C$ lie on the same straight line. The distance $AB = 75\text{ m}$. Find the height of the church tower.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: Draw a horizontal line through $A$ and $B$ to the foot of the tower and let the horizontal distance from $B$ to the tower be $x$; use $\tan$ in right-angled triangles from $A$ and $B$ to form two equations in $x$ and the height $h$, then solve for $h$.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: Let $x$ be the horizontal distance from $B$ to the foot of the tower and $h$ the height; then from $B$, $\tan32^\circ=\dfrac{h}{x}\Rightarrow h=x\tan32^\circ$; from $A$, the horizontal distance is $x+75$ so $\tan15^\circ=\dfrac{h}{x+75}$; substituting $h$ gives $\tan15^\circ=\dfrac{x\tan32^\circ}{x+75}$ which rearranges to $x\tan32^\circ=\tan15^\circ(x+75)$; solving for $x$ gives $x=\dfrac{75\tan15^\circ}{\tan32^\circ-\tan15^\circ}\approx56.3\text{ m}$; hence $h=x\tan32^\circ\approx56.3\times\tan32^\circ\approx35.2\text{ m}$, so the tower is approximately $35.2\text{ m}$ high.

Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Smallest angle of a triangle with sides $7,9,12$
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB=7$ cm, $BC=9$ cm and $AC=12$ cm. Find the size of the smallest angle.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.hint: The smallest angle is opposite the smallest side. Apply the cosine rule.
Chapter 9-Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: The smallest side is $AB=7$, so smallest angle is $\angle C$. $7^{2}=9^{2}+12^{2}-2(9)(12)\cos C$. $49=81+144-216\cos C$. $216\cos C=176$. $\cos C=0.815$. $C\approx35^\circ$.
